newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico proposes $1.26 billion more for security.
newsitem.headline: Mexico proposes $1.26 billion more for security.

text.p: The Mexican government plans to boost public security spending by 10 billion pesos ($1.26 billion) over the next four years, but Mexicans from pundits to policemen said Tuesday that simply throwing money at the issue is not enough.

"The point is not how much will be spent, but how it will be used," said political analyst Luis Rubio, of the independent think tank Development Research Centre. "If they're going to make police more accountable, that might be better than hiring more poorly paid officers."
The plan to boost security spending was proposed Monday by the National Public Security Council, which is made up of Mexico's interior ministry and state governors.

The usually acquiescent Mexican Congress in coming days will decide whether to approve an additional 2.4 billion pesos ($303 million) for the 1997 security budget. The money would have to be siphoned off other government programmes.

Violent crime has surged dramatically since the economic crisis brought on by the December 1994 peso devaluation, which threw more than a million people out of work. Those jobs are only now being recovered, according to government figures.
Mexicans tend to be wary of the police, who are widely seen as using corruption to supplement their meagre salaries.
The pledge to spend more to fight crime follows the appointment of army officers to some key Mexico City police posts and comes just as the government is due to release its 1997 budget Thursday.

Hector Teran Teran, the governor of Baja California state where drug gangs are especially active, said the proposed spending increase is not nearly enough. Others questioned which programmes would be cut to find the money.
Cops on the street, many of whom have to buy their own equipment and traditionally bribe their own superiors for lucrative or cushy assignments, said they appreciated the promise of better back-up.

"There is something very important about this and that is that they'll be able to hire more officers," one police officer walking the beat in Mexico City said. "More officers, more arms, more equipment."
Under the plan, the federal government would assume 80 percent of the additional costs with the rest being picked up by Mexico's 31 states and Mexico City's Federal District.
